editorial_examples.english: The mime’s body language appears very controlled.
editorial_examples.note: Corrected the misspelling and English translation; the revised sentence uses the adjective naturally.

editorial_examples.english: What time does the shopping mall close?
editorial_examples.note: Corrected the standard separated spelling “wie viel” and used a natural English equivalent.
Replaced archaic wording with a concise modern German sentence.

editorial_examples.german: Schütteln Sie die Flasche vor Gebrauch.
editorial_examples.note: Replaced a label fragment with a complete, polite imperative sentence.

editorial_examples.english: You may refuse the treatment at any time. In that case, however, I must explain the possible effects to you.
editorial_examples.note: Corrected the translation to match the German precisely and removed the duplicated, awkward English phrasing.

editorial_examples.german: Manche Fische können ihr Geschlecht wechseln.
editorial_examples.note: Corrected the biological English sense: in this context Geschlecht means sex, not gender.

entry_updates.value: admission, entrance fee/access; occurrence or beginning of something
entry_updates.note: Expanded the gloss to cover the clearly attested free-admission sense in the retained example, while preserving the event/occurrence sense.
Added the sense “affected” required by the flood example; retained the emotional sense.
Corrected the headword part of speech. Misstrauisch is an adjective used adverbially in this sentence.
Aligned the gloss with the adjective headword and clarified its adverbial use in the example.

entry_updates.value: to chat, talk casually; colloquially, to talk nonsense
entry_updates.note: Added the common colloquial sense “chat/talk casually” used by the replacement example and retained the talk-nonsense sense with its register.
Made the informal register explicit and replaced the unclear “freaked out” gloss.
